Evaluate the line integral ${\int }_{C}16xy\,\text{d}s,$ where the curve $C$ is the quarter of the ellipse ${x}^{2}+9{y}^{2}=9$  traversed from the point $(0,1)$ to the point $(-3,0).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14057969/assets/fda8bfb0533b86dc4050d1b8e309e332996b26263b1052d3e251bf0a5c98e816.png)

Evaluate the line integral $\displaystyle\int_\limits{C}12xy\:\textrm{d}s,$ where the curve $C$ is the quarter-ellipse $4x^2+y^2=4$ traversed from the point $(0,2)$ to the point $(-1,0),$ as shown above.
examples.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}s  = \int\limits_a^b  f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
x^2 + \dfrac{y^2}{2^2}  = 1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $1$ and $2,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \big\langle \cos{t}, \: 2\sin{t} \big\rangle, \qquad \dfrac{\pi}{2} \le t \le \pi.
$$

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t)$ and $\| \mathbf{r}'(t) \|,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t+4{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{3{cos}^{2}⁡t+({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{1+3{cos}^{2}⁡t}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y) = 12xy$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =12\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot 2\operatorname{sin}⁡t=24\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}12xy\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }24\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \sqrt{1+3{cos}^{2}⁡t}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =24{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{1+3{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=1+3\cos^2 {t},$ $\textrm d u=-6\sin t\cos 
 t\,\textrm d t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}24{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{1+3{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t & =-4{\int }_{1}^{4}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-4\cdot \frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}{|}_{1}^{4} \\  & =-\frac{8}{3}({4}^{3/2}-{1}^{3/2}) \\  & =-\frac{8}{3}(8-1) \\  & =-\frac{56}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14057969/assets/1e09fa361aca812f22d9d28430a8584e069c0eb9a2aa90f5e665d892dddd378f.png)

Which of the following gives the line integral ${\int }_{C}(5-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s,$ where the curve $C$ is three-quarters of the ellipse $5{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=5,$ shown above?
feedback.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{(\sqrt{5})^{2}}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $1$ and $\sqrt{5},$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t\le \frac{3\pi }{2}.
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t+5{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{4{cos}^{2}⁡t+({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{4{cos}^{2}⁡t+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=5-{y}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =5-(\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =5-5{sin}^{2}⁡t \\  & =5(1-{sin}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =5{cos}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(5-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}5{cos}^{2}⁡t\sqrt{4{cos}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =5{\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}{cos}^{2}⁡t\sqrt{4{cos}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$
